Subject: Follow-up: Pricing & batching assumptions — ACME Platform

Hi Alice / team,

Thanks again for the call today — appreciate the clear run-through of your inference patterns. Quick recap + asks so we can align on a preliminary pricing estimate: 

Summary of what I heard from the call:
- Monthly token volume: ~150M–300M tokens (pilot -> Q4 target).
- Typical request pattern: many short prompts (20–120 tokens) for interactive UI flows, plus occasional long batch jobs (5k–20k tokens) for nightly scoring.
- Target unit economics: aiming for ~$12–18 / 1M tokens (all-in) at scale (looking for confirmation if this is realistic).
- SLA/latency expectations: 95th perc < 400ms for interactive paths; batch jobs can tolerate higher latency.
- Concurrency: peak 250 concurrent interactive sessions; average inter-arrival time ~200–400ms per session.

Key assumption we need you to confirm:
1) Continuous batching: you expect requests to flow steadily from the UI (not large bursts), so runtime can maintain continuous batching across many small requests — is that accurate?
2) Session stickiness: do you expect clients to reuse the same session/context frequently (so KV cache hit rates are high)?
3) For the long nightly jobs, are they windowed (e.g., 01:00–04:00 UTC) or spread out?

Next steps:
- Aditya will propose a preliminary unit-cost model that includes an assumed batching factor and concurrency headroom.
- If you confirm the continuous-batching and KV cache assumptions, we can target the $12–18 / 1M tokens band for a dedicated configuration and provide an example monthly estimate in the attached sheet.

Attachments: acme_example_unit_econ.xlsx (worked example of unit economics); redwood_billing_disclaimer.pdf

Thanks — LMK any corrections to the recap and the three confirms above.

Best,
Marissa

Hi Marissa,

Thanks for the summary — that's spot on. A few clarifications: 

- Monthly volume: aim is 200M tokens in steady-state (we're budgeting for 150–250M initially).
- Interactive prompts: median ~40 tokens; 90th ~120 tokens. Most sessions are active users in the web app; they do reuse session contexts during a single user session (so KV caching should help).
- Nightly jobs: yes, they run in a 2–3 hour window (02:00–05:00 UTC) and are fairly parallel; they can be scheduled to avoid our peak interactive window.
- Bursts: we expect occasional spikes (e.g., marketing events) that could increase interactive concurrency to ~350 for short periods.

Regarding target unit economics: $12–18 / 1M tokens is the internal goal. We are hoping Redwood can demonstrate that with a dedicated plan and batching/caching assumptions. If you can show an example with conservative (not best-case) batching factors that still lands near $15 / 1M tokens, that would be ideal.

Happy to have a short follow-up with Aditya to sync on technical assumptions.

Hi Alice — thanks, and great details. A quick technical note on the batching and concurrency assumptions and how they map to unit economics. I put the short version here; see attached workbook for worked numbers.

Assumptions we used for the estimate: 
- Model: open LLM (example quantized variant) with throughput ~120 tokens/sec per GPU for interactive paths (varies by model/quant).
- Continuous batching behavior: since inter-arrival times are small (~200–400ms) and many sessions are concurrent, the runtime achieves an effective batching factor of ~6–10 for short requests (40–120 tokens). That means per-request overhead amortizes across ~6–10 requests typically in the steady state.
- Effective tokenization overhead: short prompts have higher per-token overhead; we modelled 1.2x overhead for median 40-token prompts vs long-form.
- KV cache hit rate: with session reuse, assume 60–75% cache hits for the interactive context (reduces decode time significantly).
- Peak concurrency headroom: we size for 350 concurrent interactive sessions and autoscale buffers for short spikes.

Cost math (illustrative):
- Baseline infra unit cost (GPU + infra + infra ops) per GPU-hour: $12 (example committed rate).
- Effective tokens/sec per GPU (accounting for batching+kv): ~650 tokens/sec steady for mixed interactive load.
- Tokens per GPU-hour: 650 * 3600 = ~2.34M tokens/hr.
- Hourly cost/token = $12 / 2.34M = $0.00513 per 1k tokens => $5.13 per 1M tokens (infra only).
- Add model + storage + networking + margin (~2.0–2.5x) => estimated $11–13 / 1M tokens.

Notes & caveats:
- If batch jobs dominate and are scheduled into off-peak windows, we can use higher batch sizes for those and push unit cost lower on the nightly workload.
- Short bursts with empty caches reduce effective batching on the tail and increase unit costs temporarily; our pricing proposal includes a small buffer to account for that.
- These numbers are illustrative; I'll produce a detailed per-scenario sheet (pilot, steady-state, peak-event) based on the ranges you provided.

If that aligns with your expectations, I'll schedule a 30-minute follow-up next week to walk through the workbook and the autoscaling/burst policy.

Thanks,
Aditya

Aditya — this is very helpful. The infra-only math getting to ~$5.1 / 1M tokens makes sense, and the 2.0–2.5x multiplier aligns with our internal models to get to ~$11–13. A couple of quick questions before the workbook walk: 

1) For the interactive path, are you assuming continuous batching across GPUs (cross-instance batching) or batching limited to the same GPU instance? We ask because our infra team is evaluating cross-instance batching complexity.
2) For caching: do you include prefix caching only or do you assume reusable KV cache so repeated decode tokens are avoided fully on hits?

If you can confirm those two points, we can lock the $15 / 1M target for a Dedicated pilot (pending legal/PO).

Best,
Alice

Hi Alice — quick answers: 

1) Batching: Redwood's runtime supports cross-instance request aggregation within a defined routing pool for Dedicated customers (we call it the shared batch pool). That allows short requests hitting different worker instances to be aggregated into the same kernel invocation when latency SLOs allow. For the numbers above we assumed cross-instance aggregation with an effective batching window of ~50–150ms. If you cannot accept cross-instance aggregation, assume the effective batching factor drops ~25–40% depending on arrival skew.

2) Caching: we assume a reusable KV cache (decoder-side) — hits avoid re-decoding prefix tokens and significantly reduce decode compute. Our 60–75% hit-rate assumption is aligned to session reuse in your UX.

We'll put these explicit assumptions in the workbook and show a sensitivity table (cross-instance vs instance-local batching; 50% vs 75% cache hit rates) so you can see how the $/1M moves. I'll send the updated sheet and a calendar invite for the walkthrough.

Thanks,
Aditya
